collection.title: States, clinical assessment, and consciousness-measurement breadth packet
collection.scope: Distinct attributable state constructs, assessment instruments, experimental paradigms, psychometric frameworks, and expert evidential positions spanning disorders of consciousness, anesthesia, sleep and dreaming, psychedelic and contemplative states, interoception and metacognition, development, comparative consciousness, and neural measurement.
collection.method: Human-curated candidate selection followed by exact name and alias collision checks against every extant catalog shard, DOI resolution against Crossref, and source-level boundary review.
collection.boundary_policy: Every record states whether it is a state construct, assessment instrument, experimental paradigm, signal statistic, or evidential declaration; none is silently promoted to a causal or constitutive theory of consciousness.
collection.citation_policy: Each record retains at least two exact HTTPS primary, validation, systematic-review, guideline, or official locators. DOI metadata are resolved at build time; official declarations are manually verified.
collection.attribution_policy: Claims remain local to named authors, instruments, paradigms, and documents. No inferred compatibility, causal relationship, ranking, or synthesis is asserted.
collection.deduplication_policy: Names and aliases are normalized and compared with catalog.json and every catalog supplement present at build time; conceptual neighbors are retained only when their target and method are independently bounded.

records.name: Coma Recovery Scale–Revised
records.status_note: The named construct has a traceable operational literature, but its output must be interpreted with convergent behavioral, clinical, or physiological evidence.
records.summary: The CRS-R samples auditory, visual, motor, oromotor-verbal, communication, and arousal behaviors with hierarchically ordered items used to support differential diagnosis and track recovery after severe brain injury.
records.scope: Standardized bedside detection and longitudinal description of behaviors relevant to coma, unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, minimally conscious state, and emergence.
records.boundary_note: A CRS-R score is an operational behavioral assessment, not a direct meter of phenomenal consciousness and not a causal theory of consciousness.

claim_scope.target: Standardized bedside detection and longitudinal description of behaviors relevant to coma, unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, minimally conscious state, and emergence.
claim_scope.level: Bedside behavioral and diagnostic assessment.
claim_scope.does_not_establish: A CRS-R score is an operational behavioral assessment, not a direct meter of phenomenal consciousness and not a causal theory of consciousness.

basis: The original revision reported reliability and diagnostic utility across six functional subscales.
An evidence-based systematic review identified the CRS-R as the strongest-supported standardized DoC scale in its review period.
limitations: Motor, sensory, language, fatigue, medication, and fluctuating arousal can conceal awareness.
Repeated testing improves sensitivity but does not eliminate false-negative behavioral diagnoses.
evidence_profile.independence: The citation set pairs a defining or validation source with an independent validation, systematic assessment, or authoritative comparison where available.

open_questions: How many repeated assessments optimize detection without impractical burden?
Which neural measures add independent diagnostic information to CRS-R profiles?

records.name: Glasgow Coma Scale
records.status_note: The named construct has a traceable operational literature, but its output must be interpreted with convergent behavioral, clinical, or physiological evidence.
records.summary: The GCS separately grades eye, verbal, and motor responses to provide a compact, repeatable description of acute impaired responsiveness and neurological severity.

records.boundary_note: The GCS measures observable responsiveness and injury severity; it neither diagnoses every disorder of consciousness nor establishes absence of experience.

limitations: Intubation, aphasia, sedation, sensory loss, and focal motor injury can make components untestable or misleading.
The summed score can hide clinically different component profiles.

open_questions: When should component profiles replace the sum in clinical decisions?
How can untestable components be represented without false precision?
